extracted.intended_audience: USPTO examiners, Office personnel, and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining what constitutes prior art, how to measure effective filing dates, and how to apply AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a) and exceptions in 102(b) when examining patentability. Includes rules for patents, printed publications, public use, on sale, 'otherwise available', admissions, and grace-period exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office initial burden to explain rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office bears the initial burden of explaining why the applicable statutory or regulatory requirements have not been met if a claim in an application is to be rejected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whenever a claim is rejected or an objection or requirement is made, the Office shall notify the applicant thereof and state the reasons for such rejection, objection, or requirement, and provide such information and references as may be useful to the applicant in judging of the propriety of continuing prosecution. See 35 U.S.C. 132, 37 CFR 1.104(c) and MPEP § 706.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories of prior art under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art documents and activities that may preclude patentability include: patented, described in a printed publication, in public use, on sale, or otherwise available to the public before the effective filing date of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documents/activities used to determine novelty/nonobviousness include issued patents, published applications, non-patent printed publications, evidence of public use, sale activity, or other availability. See MPEP §§ 2152.02(a)–(f).

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories of prior art under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art patent documents for 102(a)(2) are U.S. patent documents (e.g., issued patent, published U.S. application, WIPO published application) that were effectively filed before the effective filing date of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See discussion of U.S. patent documents in MPEP § 2151. Note that availability of a U.S. patent document as prior art is measured from the effective filing date of that patent document.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed publication may evidence earlier public use/sale
rubrics_metrics.description: A printed publication that does not have a sufficiently early publication date to itself qualify as prior art may be competent evidence of a previous public use, sale activity, or other availability of a claimed invention where the public use/sale does have a sufficiently early date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See In re Epstein and MPEP § 2133.03(b), subsection III.C for examples where a publication documents an earlier public activity that is the actual prior art basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(1) (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art that otherwise would be included in 102(a)(1) shall not be prior art if it falls within exceptions of 102(b)(1): disclosures made one year or less before the effective filing date may be excepted if they meet specified conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 102(b)(1) subsections (A) and (B) set out specific conditions (inventor-originated disclosures and prior public disclosures by inventor-origination). See MPEP § 2153 for detailed treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specifics of 102(b)(1)(A) — inventor or derived-from-inventor disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclosure made 1 year or less before the effective filing date shall not be prior art if the disclosure was made by the inventor or joint inventor or by another who obtained the subject matter disclosed directly or indirectly from the inventor or a joint inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the grace-period inventor-originated disclosure exception; evidence necessary to show disclosure origin requires case-by-case treatment. See MPEP § 2153.01 and § 2153.01(a)/(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specifics of 102(b)(1)(B) — prior public disclosure by inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclosure made 1 year or less before the effective filing date shall not be prior art if the subject matter disclosed had, before such disclosure, been publicly disclosed by the inventor or a joint inventor or another who obtained the subject matter directly or indirectly from the inventor or a joint inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covers situations where the inventor previously publicly disclosed the subject matter before a later disclosure within the one-year window; see MPEP § 2153.01(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2) for 102(a)(2)
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclosure is not prior art under 102(a)(2) if: (A) the subject matter was obtained directly or indirectly from the inventor or joint inventor; (B) the subject matter had, before being effectively filed under (a)(2), been publicly disclosed by the inventor/joint inventor or someone who obtained it from them; or (C) the prior-disclosed subject matter and the claimed invention were owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Addresses when U.S. patent documents should be disqualified as prior art against a claimed invention. See MPEP § 2153 for examples and application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective filing date of a claimed invention (35 U.S.C. 100(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: The effective filing date is the earliest of: (1) the actual filing date of the patent or application containing the claimed invention; or (2) the filing date of the earliest application for which the patent or application is entitled to a right of priority or benefit under 35 U.S.C. 119, 120, 121, 365, or 386.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The one-year grace period in AIA 102(b)(1) is measured from the filing date of any U.S. or foreign patent application to which the patent/application is entitled to benefit or priority. Effective filing date is determined claim-by-claim. See MPEP § 2152.01.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art availability of U.S. patent documents measured from effective filing date
rubrics_metrics.description: The availability of a U.S. patent document as prior art is measured from the effective filing date of the claimed invention, taking into account foreign priority and domestic benefit dates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This differs from pre-AIA practice where availability might be measured from the U.S. application date or invention date. See discussion of changes introduced by AIA.

rubrics_metrics.name: AIA adopts global view — no geographic limitation for public use or sale
rubrics_metrics.description: Under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) there is no geographic limitation on where prior public use or public availability occurs — it need not be 'in this country'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office personnel should consider evidence of sales/use activity regardless of where it took place. This contrasts with pre-AIA 102(b) which had 'in this country' limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catch-all 'otherwise available to the public' prior art category
rubrics_metrics.description: AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) adds a residual category: a claimed invention is not entitled to a patent if it was 'otherwise available to the public' before its effective filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allows focus on whether the disclosure was 'available to the public' rather than the means of disclosure or classification as printed publication, public use, or sale. Examples include theses, posters, internet postings, laid-open patent applications, or certain commercial transactions. See MPEP § 2152.02(e).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation: what 'described' means for printed publications/patents
rubrics_metrics.description: To anticipate under AIA 102(a)(1) or (a)(2), a prior art document must disclose 'each and every element of the claimed invention' either explicitly or inherently, and the elements must be 'arranged or combined in the same way as in the claim.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Additionally the prior art must enable a person of ordinary skill in the art to make the invention without undue experimentation (enablement-from-POA viewpoint). There is no requirement that the prior art meet the 'how to use' requirement of 35 U.S.C. 112(a). Prior art that enables one species can anticipate a broader claim. See cases cited (Gleave, Eli Lilly, Vas-Cath, etc.) and MPEP § 2152.02(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patented — effective date and availability
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claimed invention was patented before the effective filing date, 102(a)(1) precludes a subsequent patent; the applicable prior art date for a patent is its grant date, except where the patent was secret as of the date rights were awarded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a patent was secret and later made available to the public (laid open), the prior art date is when it was made available. A patent that issues after the effective filing date and was not available as prior art under 102(a)(1) could still be prior art under 102(a)(2). See MPEP § 2152.02(a) and § 2126.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public use criteria under AIA 102(a)(1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A public use must occur before the effective filing date and is not geographically limited; public use encompasses uses that were accessible to the public or commercially exploited, and an inventor's own secret commercial use may also bar patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When aware of a potentially public use, an examiner should require applicant information showing the use did not make the claimed invention accessible to the public. See discussion comparing pre-AIA standards (Invitrogen, Woodland Trust, American Seating) and MPEP § 2133.03.

rubrics_metrics.name: On sale criteria under AIA 102(a)(1)
rubrics_metrics.description: On sale activity will bar patentability if the claimed invention was the subject of a commercial sale or offer for sale (not primarily for experimental purposes) and ready for patenting; under AIA the sale must have made the invention available to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contract law principles determine whether a commercial sale/offer occurred. Enablement inquiry is not applicable to whether an invention is 'on sale.' Secret sales among parties under confidentiality do not qualify as making the invention available to the public. See Pfaff and MPEP § 2133.03.

rubrics_metrics.name: No requirement that prior art be 'by others' under AIA 102(a)(1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike pre-AIA 102(a), AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) does not require that the prior art relied upon be by others; disclosures need not be 'by others' to be prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, disclosures by the inventor or those who obtained subject matter from the inventor within one year may be excluded by 102(b)(1). See MPEP § 2152.02(f).

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissions by applicant treated as prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: A statement by an applicant in the specification or made during prosecution identifying the work of another as 'prior art' is an admission which can be relied upon for both anticipation and obviousness determinations, regardless of whether the admitted prior art would otherwise qualify under AIA 102.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Riverwood Int'l Corp. v. R.A. Jones & Co. and Constant v. AMD and MPEP § 2129 for treatment of admissions as prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'disclosure' as used in AIA exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office treats 'disclosure' as a generic expression intended to encompass the documents and activities enumerated in AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a): being patented, described in a printed publication, in public use, on sale, otherwise available to the public, or being described in a U.S. patent, U.S. patent application publication, or WIPO published application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although AIA 102(a) does not use the term 'disclosure,' 102(b)(1) and (b)(2) use 'disclosure' when specifying exceptions; Office guidance clarifies intended scope. See MPEP § 2152.04.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grace period (102(b)(1)(A)) evidence and naming convention guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel will not apply a disclosure as prior art under 102(a)(1) if it: (1) was made one year or less before the effective filing date; (2) names the inventor or a joint inventor as an author/inventor; and (3) does not name additional persons as authors on a printed publication or joint inventors on a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the publication names exactly the same inventive entity (or a subset) as the application and is within one year, it is apparent as a grace-period inventor disclosure and will not be treated as prior art. If the publication names more authors than the application names as inventors, it may not be readily apparent that the publication is by the inventor and would be treated as prior art. What evidence is necessary to show inventor-origin depends on case facts. See MPEP § 2153.01(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim-by-claim effective filing date vs application-by-application AIA applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective filing dates are determined on a claim-by-claim basis (different claims may have different effective filing dates), while the determination of whether pre-AIA or AIA 35 U.S.C. 102/103 applies is made on an application-by-application basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 2152.01 and § 706.02 for interplay between claim-level effective filing dates and application-level applicability of pre-AIA vs AIA statutory regimes.
